days.title: Descent with Modification & Common Ancestry
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Define descent with modification.
  • Explain common ancestry.
  • Describe how species diverge over time.
  • Relate phylogeny to evolutionary history.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Descent with modification — species change over time and share common ancestors.
  • Common ancestry — all life shares a common ancestor.
  • Phylogeny — evolutionary history of a species.
  • Speciation — formation of new species.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Descent with Modification

Darwin proposed that species change over time through natural selection, and that all species descend from common ancestors.

B. Common Ancestry

  • All life shares fundamental features (DNA, ribosomes, ATP)
  • Similarities reflect shared ancestry
  • Differences reflect adaptations

C. Phylogeny

Phylogenetic trees show evolutionary relationships. The base represents a common ancestor; branches represent lineages.

💬 Let's Discuss

Darwin summarized evolution in three words: descent with modification. "Descent" means that species today are descended from earlier species; "modification" means that, over many generations, descendants change from their ancestors. Follow the branches back far enough and every living thing — bacteria, mushrooms, mango trees, carabaos and you — shares a common ancestor.

The strongest evidence for a single origin of life is what all organisms share at the deepest level: every cell uses DNA as its genetic material, the same genetic code (the codon AUG means methionine in a bacterium and in a human), ribosomes to make proteins, and ATP as its energy currency. It is very unlikely that all these would match by coincidence.

When populations of one species become separated and accumulate different changes, they may become unable to interbreed. This is speciation, the formation of new species, and it is how one ancestor gives rise to many descendants. The Philippines, with over 7,000 islands, is a natural laboratory: many species of tarsiers, cloud rats and hornbills evolved on separate islands from shared ancestors.

These relationships are shown in a phylogenetic tree, a branching diagram of phylogeny (evolutionary history). Branch points stand for common ancestors; tips are descendant species. Structures that look different but share an underlying pattern because of common ancestry are homologous (the arm of a human and the flipper of a whale).

Common mistake: "Humans evolved from chimpanzees." Humans and chimpanzees are cousins: both descended from a common ancestor that lived about 6–7 million years ago.

days.title: Development of Evolutionary Thought
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Trace the history of evolutionary thought.
  • Compare Lamarck's and Darwin's ideas.
  • Explain Darwin's contributions.
  • Describe the modern synthesis.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Lamarckism — inheritance of acquired characteristics (disproven).
  • Darwinism — natural selection as the mechanism of evolution.
  • Modern synthesis — combines Darwinism with genetics.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Early Thinkers

  • Linnaeus — classification system
  • Cuvier — fossils, catastrophism
  • Lamarck — inheritance of acquired characteristics
  • Malthus — populations grow faster than resources

B. Darwin & Wallace

  • Voyage of the HMS Beagle (1831–1836)
  • Observations in the Galápagos Islands
  • On the Origin of Species (1859)
  • Natural selection as the mechanism

C. Modern Synthesis

  • Combines Darwin's natural selection with Mendel's genetics
  • Explains how variation arises
  • Forms the basis of modern biology

💬 Let's Discuss

Ideas about how living things change developed over about a century, and comparing them shows how science improves.

Jean-Baptiste Lamarck (1809) was one of the first to say clearly that species change over time — an important step. But his mechanism was the inheritance of acquired characteristics: organisms change during their lifetime through use or disuse of body parts, and pass those changes to offspring. In his giraffe example, ancestors stretched their necks to reach leaves, and their slightly longer necks were inherited. We now know this is wrong for most traits: a bodybuilder's muscles or a tattoo are not passed to children, because changes in body cells do not change the DNA in gametes.

Charles Darwin sailed around the world on the HMS Beagle (1831–1836). He studied fossils, and finches and tortoises on the Galápagos Islands that differed from island to island. Combined with ideas on population growth from Malthus and on Earth's age from geologist Charles Lyell, this led him to natural selection. Alfred Russel Wallace, working in the Malay Archipelago, reached the same idea independently; their papers were presented together in 1858. Darwin's book On the Origin of Species appeared in 1859.

Darwin did not know how traits were inherited. Mendel's work, rediscovered in 1900, provided the answer. In the 1930s–40s, the modern synthesis combined natural selection with genetics, defining evolution as a change in allele frequencies in a population.

Compare giraffes: Lamarck — necks grew because of stretching; Darwin — giraffes that already had longer necks survived and reproduced more.

days.title: Evidence of Evolution
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe multiple lines of evidence for evolution.
  • Explain biogeography.
  • Describe the fossil record.
  • Explain homology and molecular evidence.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Biogeography — geographic distribution of species.
  • Fossil record — preserved remains showing past life.
  • Homology — similar structures from common ancestry.
  • Molecular evidence — DNA/protein similarities.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Lines of Evidence

TypeExample
BiogeographyIsland species resemble mainland species
Fossil recordTransitional fossils (e.g., Archaeopteryx)
Comparative anatomyHomologous structures (forelimbs of mammals)
Comparative embryologyEmbryos of related species look similar
Molecular biologyDNA/protein sequence similarities
Direct observationAntibiotic resistance in bacteria

B. Vestigial Structures

  • Structures with reduced function
  • Examples: human appendix, whale pelvic bones

💬 Let's Discuss

Evolution is supported by many independent lines of evidence that all point to the same conclusion.

Fossil record. Fossils in rock layers show life changing over time, with simpler organisms in older layers. Transitional fossils show intermediate features: Archaeopteryx had feathers like a bird but teeth, claws and a bony tail like a reptile; Tiktaalik was a fish with limb-like fins.

Comparative anatomy. Homologous structures have the same basic bone pattern but different functions — the forelimbs of humans (grasping), whales (swimming), bats (flying) and cats (walking) — showing descent from a common ancestor. Analogous structures, like the wings of insects and birds, do the same job but evolved separately; they show similar environments, not close relationship. Vestigial structures are reduced, with little or no function: the human tailbone, the pelvic bones of whales and pythons, wisdom teeth.

Comparative embryology. Early embryos of fish, chickens and humans look alike, with pharyngeal pouches and tails, revealing shared developmental genes.

Molecular biology. The more closely related two species are, the more similar their DNA and proteins. Human and chimpanzee DNA is about 98–99% identical; human and mouse proteins are less similar; human and yeast less still.

Biogeography. Species on islands resemble those on the nearest mainland, not those on islands with similar climates far away. Palawan's wildlife, for example, resembles that of Borneo, to which it was once connected.

Common mistake: using analogous structures as evidence of close relationship. Only homologous structures indicate common ancestry.

pairs.why: Biogeography studies where species are found and why.
The fossil record preserves evidence of past life.
Homologous structures share an underlying pattern from common ancestry.
Related species have similar early embryos.
Molecular evidence compares DNA and protein sequences.
Vestigial structures are reduced and have little or no function.

days.title: Inferring Evolutionary Relationships
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Use evidence to infer relationships.
  • Explain how molecular data builds trees.
  • Describe how fossils fill gaps.
  • Interpret phylogenetic trees.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Phylogenetic tree — diagram of evolutionary relationships.
  • Node — common ancestor point.
  • Clade — ancestor + all descendants.
  • Molecular clock — uses DNA differences to estimate time.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Inferring Relationships

  • Compare anatomy, embryology, DNA, fossils
  • Shared features → shared ancestry
  • More shared features → closer relationship

B. Molecular Clocks

Assume mutation rate is roughly constant over time. The more differences in DNA, the longer ago two species diverged.

C. Reading a Phylogenetic Tree

  • Nodes = common ancestors
  • Branch length = time or amount of change
  • Tips = present-day species

💬 Let's Discuss

How do scientists decide who is related to whom? They compare characters — anatomical features, behaviors and especially DNA and protein sequences — and assume that species sharing more homologous features share a more recent common ancestor.

The result is a phylogenetic tree. Read it from the root (oldest ancestor) toward the tips (present-day species). Each branching point is a node, representing a common ancestor that split into two lineages. A clade is a group made of one ancestor and all of its descendants — like a branch you could cut off with one snip. To find how closely two species are related, trace back to their most recent shared node: the more recent it is, the closer they are. The order of tips can be rotated without changing the relationships, like a mobile hanging from the ceiling.

Molecular clocks estimate when lineages split. Mutations in certain genes build up at a fairly steady rate, so the number of differences between two species' DNA indicates how long ago they diverged. Calibrated with dated fossils, this suggests that humans and chimpanzees split about 6–7 million years ago, while humans and mice split about 75–90 million years ago. Species that diverged 50 million years ago have had more time to accumulate differences than species that split 5 million years ago.

Molecular data sometimes surprise us: whales turned out to be closely related to hippopotamuses.

Common mistake: reading a tree as a ladder of "lower" to "higher" organisms. Every living species at a tip has been evolving for the same amount of time.
